sources.title: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume 1, Chapter V: The Contributing Cause of the Accident
sources.author_or_institution: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission); archived by NASA History Office
sources.supported_claim: Sequence and content of the January 27, 1986 teleconference: the forecast temperature, Thiokol's initial written recommendation against launch below 53°F, NASA Marshall's (Mulloy/Hardy) pushback, the off-line Thiokol caucus and Jerry Mason's 'management hat' remark to Robert Lund, and the reversal to a formal launch recommendation.

sources.title: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (full report)
sources.author_or_institution: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident
sources.citation: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. (1986). Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Washington, D.C.: U.S. Government Printing Office.
sources.supported_claim: Official finding that failure of the right SRB aft field-joint O-ring seal caused the accident; reconstruction of the O-ring material temperature (~28°F) at ignition; Roger Boisjoly's Commission testimony describing the reversal of the burden of proof from 'prove it is safe' to 'prove it is not safe.'

sources.title: The Challenger Launch Decision: Risky Technology, Culture, and Deviance at NASA
sources.citation: Vaughan, D. (1996). The Challenger Launch Decision: Risky Technology, Culture, and Deviance at NASA. University of Chicago Press.
sources.supported_claim: Sociological analysis of how repeated prior flights with O-ring erosion became normalized within NASA/Thiokol's risk culture ('normalization of deviance'), framing why the cold-weather warning did not automatically override schedule pressure.

sources.title: Visual Explanations: Images and Quantities, Evidence and Narrative (Chapter 2: 'Visual and Statistical Thinking')
sources.citation: Tufte, E. R. (1997). Visual Explanations: Images and Quantities, Evidence and Narrative. Cheshire, CT: Graphics Press.
sources.supported_claim: Analysis showing the O-ring erosion charts used in the January 27 teleconference organized data by launch/mission date rather than by temperature, used cluttered rocket-icon graphics, and omitted several warm-weather launches with no O-ring damage — weakening the visual case for the temperature correlation the engineers believed in.

sources.title: How record-setting cold contributed to the space shuttle Challenger disaster on Jan. 28, 1986
sources.date: Published for the disaster's anniversary; content dated to the 1986 event
sources.supported_claim: Specific launch-day conditions: overnight low near 22°F, ice on the launch pad structure, and a liftoff-time air temperature of approximately 36°F, roughly 15°F colder than any previous shuttle launch.

sources.title: Utah engineers' warning was ignored before Challenger explosion 30 years ago
sources.date: 2016 (retrospective reporting on 1986 events, drawing on Boisjoly's own accounts and testimony)
sources.supported_claim: Roger Boisjoly's and Arnold Thompson's own account of arguing against launch in the teleconference, and the exclusion of dissenting engineers from Thiokol's final go-decision.

sources.title: 'A Catastrophe of the Highest Order': The Tragic Legacy of Roger Boisjoly
sources.supported_claim: Boisjoly's post-accident testimony and interviews describing the January 27 meeting, the caucus, and his belief that the decision process had been compromised by schedule pressure.

sources.title: Challenger disaster
sources.supported_claim: General chronology cross-check: crew fatalities, the Rogers Commission's cause finding, and the roughly three-year grounding of the Shuttle program until STS-26 in September 1988.
